objectives.text: From memory, APPLY the principles of force to stationary or moving bodies.

enabling.text: STATE the purpose of a free-body diagram.
Given all necessary information, CONSTRUCT a free-body diagram.
STATE the conditions necessary for a body to be in force equilibrium.
EXPLAIN the difference between a static-friction force and a kinetic-friction force.
STATE two factors that affect the magnitude of the friction force.
EXPLAIN the difference between centripetal force and centrifugal force.

passages.quote: Force is defined as a vector quantity that tends to produce an acceleration of a body in the direction of its application.
Force is characterized by its point of application, its magnitude, and its direction.
It is defined as the force exerted on an object by the gravitational field of the earth, or more specifically the pull of the earth on the body.
The mass of a body is the same wherever the body is, whether on the moon or on the earth.
The diagram of such an isolated body with the representation of all external forces acting on it is called a Free-Body Diagram.
A normal force is defined as any perpendicular force with which any two surfaces are pressed against each other.
Do not show the forces that the object exerts on anything else, since these forces do not affect the object itself.
The force which results from all the forces acting on a body is defined as the net force.
Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of motion.
If the sum of all forces acting upon a body is equal to zero, that body is said to be in force equilibrium.
If the sum of all the forces is not equal to zero, any force or system of forces capable of balancing the system is defined as an equilibrant.
If an applied force on a member tends to pull the member apart, it is said to be in tension.
ropes, cables, etc., that are attached to bodies can only support tensile loads
fluid forces are almost always compressive forces.
Such forces are referred to as friction forces.
As soon as the block has been set in motion, the magnitude of F drops from FM to a lower value
do not depend upon the area of the surfaces in contact.
Both coefficients, however, depend strongly on the nature of the surfaces in contact.
frictional forces are always opposite in direction to the motion (or impending motion) of the object.
This force is known as centripetal force.
This is actually a fictitious force, but is an apparent force that is used to describe the forces present due to an object's rotation.

body.text: F = ma
Two or more forces may act upon an object without affecting its state of motion. A book on a table has a downward force from gravity and an upward force from the table top, and the net force is zero.
Weight is a special application of the concept of force.
W = mg / gc
W is weight in lbf, m is mass in lbm, g is the local acceleration of gravity (32.17 ft/sec²), and gc is a conversion constant equal to 32.17 ft-lbm/lbf-sec².
The weight of a body depends upon the local acceleration of gravity, so an object weighs less on the moon than on the earth.

checks.q: What three things characterize a force?
o: Its mass, velocity, and time
Its point of application, magnitude, and direction
Its length, width, and depth
Its area, volume, and density
checks.x: Force is characterized by its point of application, its magnitude, and its direction.

checks.q: A body moves from the earth to the moon. What happens to its mass and weight?
o: Mass decreases and weight stays the same
Both decrease
Mass stays the same and weight decreases
Both stay the same
checks.x: Mass is the same wherever the body is. Weight depends on the local acceleration of gravity, which is less on the moon.

body.text: To account for all the forces on a body, the body must be isolated from all other bodies.
The isolation of a body clearly separates cause and effect and focuses attention on the literal application of a principle.
A book resting on a table has its weight (W) and the normal force (N) from the table, which is equal to the weight of the book.

body.alt: A book on a table, and beside it the free-body diagram of the book with weight W pointing down and normal force N pointing up.

body.text: A free-body diagram is usually constructed in four steps:

items: Determine which body or combination of bodies is to be isolated.
Isolate it with a diagram that represents its complete external boundaries.
Represent all forces that act on the isolated body, in their proper positions.
Indicate the choice of coordinate axes directly on the diagram.

body.text: A car being towed has four forces on its diagram: the applied force, the frictional force that opposes it, the weight of the car, and the normal force from the road.

body.alt: Free-body diagram of a car with the applied force to the right, friction FK to the left, weight W down, and normal force N up.

checks.q: Which forces are left off a free-body diagram?
o: The normal force on the object
The weight of the object
Forces the object exerts on anything else
Frictional forces on the object
checks.x: Do not show the forces that the object exerts on anything else, since these forces do not affect the object itself.

body.text: Forces are vector quantities, so both the magnitude and the direction of each force must be accounted for. This is best done using a free-body diagram.

body.alt: Three views of a book on a table: at rest with zero net force, with an applied force, and a free-body diagram with N and W canceling.

body.text: Newton's first law of motion is also called the law of inertia.
ΣF = 0
This condition applies to objects in motion with constant velocity and to bodies at rest.

o: Any force or system of forces capable of balancing the system
The force of gravity on an object
The force that results from all forces acting on a body
The tendency of a body to resist a change in motion
checks.x: If the sum of all the forces is not equal to zero, any force or system of forces capable of balancing the system is defined as an equilibrant.

checks.q: How does the handbook define net force?
o: The largest single force on a body
The force which results from all the forces acting on a body
The force needed to balance a system
The perpendicular force between two surfaces
checks.x: The force which results from all the forces acting on a body is defined as the net force.

body.text: If a force tends to compress the member, it is in compression.
Forces from two surfaces in contact, where one surface is attempting to move parallel to or over the other, are friction forces.
With a small applied force, a block does not move, because the static-friction force balances the applied force.
As the applied force increases, the static-friction force increases until it reaches a maximum value, FM. Beyond that, the block starts sliding.

body.alt: A block on a surface with weight W and normal force N, then with applied force P and friction F, and a graph of friction force rising to FM and dropping to FK at motion.

body.text: That lower value, FK, is the kinetic-friction force, which remains approximately constant as the block slides.
FM = μs N
FK = μK N

checks.q: What kind of load can a cable support?
o: Compressive loads only
Tensile loads only
Both tensile and compressive loads
Frictional loads only
checks.x: Ropes, cables, and similar objects attached to bodies can only support tensile loads.

checks.q: A block that was held by static friction starts to slide. What happens to the friction force?
o: It rises above the maximum static value
It drops to zero
It stays at the maximum static value
It drops to a lower value, the kinetic-friction force
checks.x: As soon as the block has been set in motion, the magnitude of the friction force drops from FM to a lower value, FK.

checks.q: Which of these does NOT change the coefficients of friction?
o: The area of the surfaces in contact
The nature of the surfaces in contact
The exact condition of the surfaces
The type of surfaces in contact
checks.x: The coefficients of friction do not depend upon the area of the surfaces in contact. They depend strongly on the nature of the surfaces.

body.text: An object moving at constant speed in a circle is not in equilibrium, because the direction of its velocity is continually changing.
A net force acts towards the center of the circular path.
Without this force, an object will move in a straight line.

body.alt: A plane moving in a circle, with an arrow for centripetal force pointing toward the center.

body.text: Centrifugal force appears to be a force directed away from the center of the circular path.
If a string holding a plane in a circle is cut, the plane flies off in a straight line tangent to the circle. If an actual centrifugal force were present, it would fly directly away from the circle.

body.alt: A plane leaving the circular path in a straight line tangent to the circle after centripetal force goes to zero.

checks.q: How does centrifugal force differ from centripetal force?
o: Centrifugal force acts toward the center and is a real force
Centrifugal force is a fictitious force that appears directed away from the center
Both are real forces directed toward the center
Centrifugal force exists only in straight-line motion
checks.x: Centripetal force acts towards the center of the path. Centrifugal force is a fictitious, apparent force that appears to be directed away from the center.

examples.problem: An object weighing 125 lbf hangs motionless from cables. Calculate the tension T1 in the cable at 30° with the horizontal.
steps: The object is in equilibrium, so the sum of the y components is zero.
Choose + as upward. The upward component of T1 is T1 sin 30°, T3 is -125 lbf, and T2 has no y component.

facts.a: The tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of motion.
Any perpendicular force with which any two surfaces are pressed against each other.

facts.q: How does the handbook define force?
facts.a: A vector quantity that tends to produce an acceleration of a body in the direction of its application.

facts.q: What direction do frictional forces act?
facts.a: Always opposite in direction to the motion, or impending motion, of the object.

facts.q: Are fluid forces usually tensile or compressive?
facts.a: Fluid forces are almost always compressive forces.

summary.text: Force is a vector quantity that tends to produce an acceleration of a body in the direction of its application.
Weight is the force exerted on an object due to gravity.
A free-body diagram isolates a body and illustrates all the forces that act on the body.
If the vector sum of all the forces acting on an object is equal to zero, then the object is in equilibrium.
Any force or system of forces capable of balancing a system so that the net force is zero is an equilibrant.
Static-frictional forces are present when an object is stationary, and kinetic-frictional forces are present between two objects that are moving.
Centripetal force is directed towards the center of the path. Centrifugal force is a fictitious force that appears directed away from it.

blend_notes.note: The car equilibrant example prints the acceleration as 2 ft-sec. That looks like a misprint for ft/sec², so the example is not used.

Objective 1.8 asks for two factors that affect friction, but the summary lists three: weight, the surface of the object, and the surface it moves on. The check on this objective tests the coefficients instead.
Equation number 4-5 is used twice, on pages 13 and 19. The lesson does not use equation numbers.
